n0001.title: On the Origin of Species
n0001.gist: Darwin argues that all species arise and diverge from common ancestors through natural selection acting on inherited variation, and defends this theory against rival explanations from variation, instinct, hybridism, geology, distribution, and classification.

n0002.title: Front Matter and Introduction
n0002.gist: The volume opens with publication details, a full table of contents, and Darwin's personal account of how he arrived at the theory of descent with modification.

n0003.title: Publication Details
n0003.gist: The edition history, title page, and epigraphs of the book are presented before the argument begins.

n0020.title: Table of Contents
n0020.gist: A detailed chapter-by-chapter outline previews every topic the book will cover.

n0053.title: Introduction
n0053.gist: Darwin explains his decades of research, credits Wallace's independent discovery, and outlines the book's chapter-by-chapter argument for descent with modification via natural selection.

n0054.title: Origin of the Inquiry
n0054.gist: Darwin recounts how observations on the Beagle voyage and years of study led him, alongside Wallace, to publish this abstract.

n0062.title: Case Against Independent Creation
n0062.gist: He argues that adaptations like the woodpecker and misseltoe demand an explanation beyond mere external conditions, pointing toward domestication as the key clue.

n0066.title: Plan of the Argument
n0066.gist: Darwin previews how each subsequent chapter builds the case for natural selection and states his core conclusion that species are not immutable.

n0070.title: Variation and Natural Selection
n0070.gist: Darwin establishes that domestic and wild organisms vary heritably, and that a struggle for existence causes natural selection to accumulate favorable variations into new species.

n0071.title: CHAPTER I. VARIATION UNDER DOMESTICATION
n0071.gist: Domestic breeds show that heritable variation, guided by centuries of human selection, can transform organisms far beyond their wild ancestors.

n0072.title: Causes of Variability
n0072.gist: Variation arises mainly because domestic conditions disturb the reproductive system rather than acting directly on the body.

n0082.title: Inheritance and Reversion
n0082.gist: Variations tend to be inherited at the same age they first appeared, and domestic varieties can revert toward ancestral traits.

n0092.title: Origin of Domestic Pigeons
n0092.gist: Despite their extreme diversity, all pigeon breeds descend from the wild rock-pigeon, as shown by reversion and shared marks.

n0102.title: Power of Selection
n0102.gist: Breeders' patient accumulation of tiny differences, not single dramatic changes, has produced today's distinct domestic races.

n0112.title: Unconscious Selection
n0112.gist: Even without deliberate breeding programs, everyday preference for the best individuals steadily reshapes a breed over generations.

n0122.title: Summary: Domestic Races
n0122.gist: Variability, inheritance, and cumulative selection together explain the origin of all our domestic races.

n0126.title: CHAPTER II. VARIATION UNDER NATURE
n0126.gist: Wild species show the same graduated variability as domestic ones, blurring the line between varieties and species, especially in large, widespread genera.

n0127.title: Variability and Individual Differences
n0127.gist: Individual differences within species supply the raw material that natural selection can later act upon.

n0137.title: Species or Variety Distinction
n0137.gist: No firm line separates variety from species, and naturalists' judgments on doubtful forms shift with experience.

n0146.title: Dominant Species in Larger Genera
n0146.gist: Species in larger genera vary more and resemble each other more closely, treating species as advanced varieties.

n0155.title: CHAPTER III. STRUGGLE FOR EXISTENCE
n0155.gist: Because organisms multiply geometrically but resources are finite, every being faces a constant struggle for life that sets the stage for selection.

n0156.title: Struggle for Existence Introduced
n0156.gist: Darwin defines the struggle for existence broadly, including dependence and reproductive success, not just death.

n0165.title: Geometrical Ratio of Increase
n0165.gist: Every organism tends to increase at a geometrical rate, so unchecked populations would rapidly overrun the earth.

n0174.title: Checks on Increase
n0174.gist: Climate, food supply, and competitors interact in complex, often indirect ways to limit each species' numbers.

n0183.title: Nature of the Checks
n0183.gist: Competition is fiercest between similar organisms, so the structure of each being is shaped by its relations to others.

n0189.title: CHAPTER IV. NATURAL SELECTION
n0189.gist: Natural selection, aided by sexual selection and divergence of character, gradually transforms varieties into distinct species and drives the branching tree of life.

n0190.title: Natural Selection Defined
n0190.gist: Natural selection preserves favorable variations and rejects harmful ones, acting far more powerfully and precisely than human selection.

n0202.title: Sexual Selection and Illustrations
n0202.gist: Competition among males for mates adds another selective force, illustrated by imagined cases like wolves and their prey.

n0206.title: Coadaptation of Flowers and Insects
n0206.gist: Mutual benefit between flowers and pollinating insects shows how natural selection can craft intricate reciprocal adaptations.

n0221.title: On Intercrossing of Individuals
n0221.gist: Even hermaphrodites likely benefit from occasional crossing, which natural selection favors because it boosts vigor.

n0231.title: Circumstances Favouring Selection
n0231.gist: Large populations, variability, and moderate isolation together create the best conditions for natural selection to act.

n0241.title: Extinction and Divergence
n0241.gist: As improved forms spread, they drive their less-fit relatives extinct while diverging into ever more specialized niches.

n0251.title: Diagram of Divergence
n0251.gist: A branching diagram shows how one ancestral species can generate many divergent, extinction-pruned descendant species and genera.

n0261.title: Summary: Natural Selection
n0261.gist: Natural selection, extinction, and divergence together explain the branching, hierarchical structure of all life, likened to a great tree.

n0270.title: Laws of Variation and Theoretical Difficulties
n0270.gist: Darwin details the largely unknown laws governing variation, then confronts and answers the gravest objections to natural selection, from complex organs to sterile ant castes.

n0271.title: CHAPTER V. LAWS OF VARIATION
n0271.gist: Variation is shaped by use and disuse, correlation of growth, and reversion, and specific traits vary more readily than deeply inherited generic ones.

n0272.title: Causes of Variability Revisited
n0272.gist: Climate and habitat produce only minor direct effects on organisms compared with the disturbed reproductive system.

n0284.title: Effects of Use and Disuse
n0284.gist: Disused organs like eyes in cave animals or wings in island beetles shrink through inherited habit and selection.

n0295.title: Acclimatisation
n0295.gist: Species can become habituated to new climates through a flexible constitution, aided by both habit and selection.

n0304.title: Correlation of Growth
n0304.gist: Changes to one part of an organism often necessarily alter other, seemingly unrelated parts through developmental linkage.

n0313.title: Specific vs Generic Variability
n0313.gist: Traits that distinguish species from their close relatives are more variable than the deep traits shared across a whole genus.

n0325.title: Analogous Variation and Reversion
n0325.gist: Related species vary in similar ways and can revert to ancestral characters, as shown by striped horses and pigeon plumage.

n0330.title: CHAPTER VI. DIFFICULTIES ON THEORY
n0330.gist: Darwin confronts the missing transitional forms, complex organs like the eye, and imperfect adaptations, arguing none disprove gradual natural selection.

n0331.title: Difficulties Stated
n0331.gist: Darwin lays out the chief objections: missing transitional forms, complex organs, instinct, and hybrid sterility.

n0342.title: Absence of Transitional Varieties
n0342.gist: Transitional forms are rare today because new, improved varieties tend to supplant and exterminate their less-fit parents.

n0397.title: Range and Neutral Zones
n0397.gist: Species ranges are sharply bounded because competition, not gradually shifting climate, controls where organisms can persist.

n0399.title: CHAPTER VII. INSTINCT
n0399.gist: Even astonishing instincts like slave-making ants and honeycomb-building bees can arise through natural selection acting on small variations in behavior.

n0400.title: Instinct Compared with Habit
n0400.gist: Instincts resemble inherited habits, but most complex instincts cannot simply be habits acquired within one generation.

n0413.title: Domestic Instincts
n0413.gist: Bred behaviors like pointing or tumbling show that instincts vary and can be selected just like physical traits.

n0419.title: Cuckoo and Parasitic Instincts
n0419.gist: The cuckoo's egg-laying habit likely arose from an ancestor's occasional practice becoming advantageous and inherited.

n0423.title: Slave-Making Ants
n0423.gist: Darwin's direct observations of Formica sanguinea show a slave-making instinct plausibly built up from an ancestral habit of storing pupae as food.

n0431.title: Cell-Making Instinct of Bees
n0431.gist: The hive-bee's geometrically perfect comb can be explained by simple instincts to excavate equal, intersecting spheres economically.

n0446.title: Neuter Insects and Summary
n0446.gist: Sterile worker castes, seemingly fatal to the theory, are explained by selection acting on the fertile parents of a whole colony.

n0459.title: Hybridism and the Fossil Record
n0459.gist: Darwin shows that hybrid sterility is an incidental byproduct of divergence rather than a special barrier, and that the imperfect fossil record explains the apparent gaps between species.

n0460.title: CHAPTER VIII. HYBRIDISM
n0460.gist: The sterility of species crosses and the fertility of variety crosses graduate into each other, showing sterility is incidental rather than a divinely fixed barrier between species.

n0461.title: Sterility of Crosses vs Hybrids
n0461.gist: Darwin distinguishes sterility of first crosses between species from the separate phenomenon of hybrid offspring sterility.

n0471.title: Variable Fertility of Hybrids
n0471.gist: Careful experiments by Kölreuter, Gärtner, and Herbert reveal that hybrid fertility varies enormously and even sometimes exceeds normal fertility.

n0478.title: Laws of Sterility
n0478.gist: Sterility of crosses graduates continuously and does not strictly track systematic affinity between the species involved.

n0485.title: Causes of Sterility
n0485.gist: Sterility likely arises from disturbed reproductive systems, paralleling how new or unnatural conditions of life also cause sterility.

n0498.title: Parallelism with Conditions of Life
n0498.gist: Just as changed conditions can impair fertility, crossing distinct organizations disturbs development in a directly analogous way.

n0502.title: Varieties, Mongrels, and Summary
n0502.gist: Because varieties are usually fertile when crossed and resemble hybrids in every other respect, no fundamental line separates species from varieties.

n0522.title: CHAPTER IX. ON THE IMPERFECTION OF THE GEOLOGICAL RECORD
n0522.gist: Vast lapses of time, poor fossil preservation, and intermittent deposition mean the rock record is far too incomplete to show the countless transitional links descent requires.

n0523.title: Absence of Living Transitional Forms
n0523.gist: Missing intermediate links are expected because extinction constantly removes the parent forms and connecting varieties.

n0531.title: Lapse of Time
n0531.gist: Geological evidence of denudation and sedimentation reveals almost incomprehensibly vast spans of time available for slow modification.

n0542.title: Poor Palaeontological Record
n0542.gist: Fossil collections are sparse and biased, preserving only a tiny, patchy sample of past life.

n0546.title: Intermittent Formations
n0546.gist: Sediment accumulates thick enough to survive only during subsidence, so formations are separated by immense unrecorded gaps.

n0568.title: Sudden Appearance of Groups
n0568.gist: Whole groups seem to appear abruptly only because they evolved and spread elsewhere before entering the well-explored regions.

n0575.title: Lowest Known Strata
n0575.gist: The absence of fossils beneath the Silurian strata remains unexplained but is attributed to metamorphism or unexplored ancient continents.

n0583.title: CHAPTER X. ON THE GEOLOGICAL SUCCESSION OF ORGANIC BEINGS
n0583.gist: The slow, non-simultaneous, non-repeating appearance and extinction of species and groups in the fossil record matches exactly what descent with modification predicts.

n0584.title: Slow Successive Appearance
n0584.gist: New species appear gradually rather than simultaneously, and different lineages change at markedly different rates.

n0594.title: Extinction
n0594.gist: Extinction is the near-inevitable consequence of new, better-adapted forms outcompeting and replacing their predecessors.

n0602.title: Simultaneous Change Worldwide
n0602.gist: Forms of life change in loose worldwide unison because dominant species spread and supplant others across whole regions.

n0612.title: Affinities of Extinct Forms
n0612.gist: Ancient and extinct species often sit intermediate in character between modern groups, exactly as branching descent predicts.

n0625.title: Development of Ancient Forms
n0625.gist: Later forms of life tend to be more advanced than their defeated ancient predecessors, and embryos may preserve traces of ancestral structure.

n0629.title: Succession of Types and Summary
n0629.gist: Living and extinct species of the same region share the same body plans, showing that descent, not fixed law, governs succession.

n0642.title: Distribution, Classification, and Development
n0642.gist: Migration and modification, not independent creation, explain the geography of life, and shared descent underlies classification, anatomy, embryology, and vestigial organs.

n0643.title: CHAPTER XI. GEOGRAPHICAL DISTRIBUTION
n0643.gist: Barriers, not climate, chiefly explain where organisms live, and migration from single centers—especially during the Glacial period—accounts for their present ranges.

n0644.title: Distribution Independent of Climate
n0644.gist: Regions with nearly identical climates can have utterly different faunas, showing physical conditions alone don't explain distribution.

n0654.title: Centres of Creation
n0654.gist: Each species most plausibly originated in a single area and migrated outward, rather than being created independently at multiple points.

n0660.title: Means of Dispersal
n0660.gist: Seeds and small animals can cross oceans via currents, floating debris, and birds far more often than previously assumed.

n0670.title: Glacial Period Dispersal
n0670.gist: A worldwide Ice Age explains why identical or closely allied Alpine and arctic species now sit isolated on distant mountains and poles.

n0684.title: Alpine Floras and Summary
n0684.gist: Mountain floras worldwide echo northern temperate forms, confirming a single great migration event driven by past climate change.

n0696.title: CHAPTER XII. GEOGRAPHICAL DISTRIBUTION—continued
n0696.gist: Freshwater life disperses surprisingly widely via birds and floods, and oceanic islands' sparse, peculiar inhabitants reveal colonization from the nearest mainland followed by local modification.

n0697.title: Fresh-water Productions
n0697.gist: Fresh-water species range widely because birds, floods, and adhering mud transport their eggs and seeds between basins.

n0706.title: Inhabitants of Oceanic Islands
n0706.gist: Oceanic islands have few but often highly endemic species, and lack whole groups like mammals and frogs that cannot cross open sea.

n0713.title: Island Affinities to Mainland
n0713.gist: Island inhabitants consistently resemble those of the nearest continent, betraying their colonization and subsequent local modification.

n0724.title: Summary of Distribution
n0724.gist: Migration, isolation, and modification together explain every major pattern of geographic distribution better than independent creation.

n0734.title: CHAPTER XIII. MUTUAL AFFINITIES OF ORGANIC BEINGS
n0734.gist: Shared descent, not an unknown creative plan, explains classification, homologous anatomy, embryonic resemblance, and useless rudimentary organs.

n0735.title: Classification and Natural System
n0735.gist: The nested, branching grouping of species into genera and families follows naturally from divergence and extinction within a single lineage.

n0739.title: Rules of Classification
n0739.gist: Naturalists value traits by their constancy and correlation rather than by physiological importance alone, a puzzle that inheritance resolves.

n0746.title: Descent as Basis of Classification
n0746.gist: Just as descent already groups sexes and varieties together, genealogy is the hidden bond that underlies all natural classification.

n0755.title: Analogy vs True Affinity; Morphology
n0755.gist: Superficial adaptive resemblance differs sharply from true blood-relationship, and shared skeletal patterns across species reveal common ancestry.

n0775.title: Embryology Fundamentals
n0775.gist: Embryos of related species resemble each other far more than the adults do, since specialization usually appears late in development.

n0782.title: Embryonic Resemblance in Domesticated Forms
n0782.gist: Measurements of young dogs, horses, and pigeons show that breed differences develop mostly after birth, supporting the theory of late-appearing variation.

n0792.title: Rudimentary Organs and Summary
n0792.gist: Useless vestigial organs, otherwise inexplicable, are naturally explained as remnants reduced by disuse and preserved through inheritance.

n0807.title: CHAPTER XIV. RECAPITULATION AND CONCLUSION
n0807.gist: Darwin reviews all the difficulties and evidence, then closes with the sweeping claim that the grandeur of life's diversity springs from a few simple, still-acting natural laws.

n0808.title: Recap of Difficulties
n0808.gist: Darwin restates the objections about hybrid sterility, missing links, and geographic puzzles, and reaffirms his earlier answers to them.

n0818.title: Recap of Supporting Evidence
n0818.gist: Domestic variation and struggle for existence together make natural selection's power to reshape species seem highly probable.

n0830.title: Struggle and Selection Recap
n0830.gist: Geometric population growth ensures relentless struggle, giving natural selection endless opportunity to favor any useful variation.

n0838.title: Instinct and Hybridism Recap
n0838.gist: Instincts and hybrid sterility follow the same graduated, inherited patterns as physical traits, fitting naturally into the theory.

n0841.title: Geology and Distribution Recap
n0841.gist: The imperfect fossil record and worldwide patterns of migration and affinity both confirm descent with modification.

n0853.title: Concluding Remarks
n0853.gist: Darwin closes by declaring that all life's beauty and complexity has evolved from simple ancestral forms through ordinary, still-operating natural laws.
